lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: Margins were your first ratios
option_a: Back in Unit 5, gross, operating, and net margin were your first taste of ratio analysis — a profit figure divided by revenue, turned into a comparable percentage.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: This unit builds outward from there
option_a: Beyond margins, this unit adds ratios that measure returns on what a company owns (ROA, ROE) and how efficiently it uses its assets (turnover ratios) — a fuller profitability and efficiency toolkit.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: A financial ratio takes two numbers from the statements and divides them, turning raw figures into a comparable measure of performance.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: Which of these is an example of a ratio you already learned, back in Unit 5?
option_a: Total revenue
option_b: Net margin (net income ÷ revenue)
option_c: Total assets
option_d: Cash balance
hint: Which of these is a single number, and which is a division of two numbers?
explanation: Net margin — net income divided by revenue — is a ratio, exactly the pattern this whole unit builds on: take two numbers, divide, get a comparable measure.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: Why are ratios generally more useful for comparing companies than raw financial figures?
option_a: Raw figures are always superior for any comparison
option_b: Ratios neutralize differences in company size, making performance comparable across companies of very different scales
option_c: Ratios are only used by regulators, never analysts
option_d: There's no real difference between ratios and raw figures
hint: Recall the margins lesson's explanation for why percentages beat raw rupee comparisons.
explanation: Just as margins let you compare a small company's profitability to a giant's fairly, ratios in general strip out the effect of sheer size, letting you compare efficiency and returns on a level footing.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: A ratio is calculated by dividing one financial figure by another.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Is that literally what a ratio, mathematically, is?
explanation: That's the basic mechanic behind every ratio in this unit — two numbers, divided, producing one comparable measure.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: This unit is titled 'Profitability & Efficiency.' Based on the intro cards, which of these best fits the 'efficiency' half?
option_a: Net margin
option_b: Return on Equity
option_c: A turnover ratio measuring how effectively assets generate sales
option_d: Gross margin
hint: Which of these measures how well resources are being used, rather than how much profit is being made per rupee of sales?
explanation: Turnover ratios (covered later in this unit) measure how efficiently a company's assets are being put to work generating sales — the 'efficiency' half of this unit's title, distinct from the pure profitability of a margin.

lesson_title: Margins as Ratios: A Quick Recap
question_or_heading: Why does this course revisit margins briefly before introducing new ratios like ROA and ROE?
option_a: Because margins and the new ratios are completely unrelated concepts
option_b: Because margins are the simplest example of the 'divide two numbers for a comparable measure' pattern that every new ratio in this unit will follow
option_c: Repetition is used here purely as a memorization trick with no conceptual purpose
option_d: Margins are actually being replaced and will no longer be used
hint: What foundational pattern do margins establish that the rest of this unit builds directly on?
explanation: Margins already established the core ratio-analysis pattern — divide two numbers, get something comparable — so revisiting them briefly sets up exactly the mental model the rest of this unit's new ratios will reuse.

question_or_heading: How much profit per rupee of assets?
option_a: Return on Assets = Net Income ÷ Total Assets. It measures how efficiently a company turns everything it owns into profit, regardless of how those assets were financed.

question_or_heading: Higher generally means more efficient
option_a: A higher ROA suggests the company is generating more profit from each rupee tied up in assets — though capital-light businesses naturally post higher ROA than capital-heavy ones.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Return on Assets = Net Income ÷ Total Assets — how much profit a company generates for every rupee of assets it owns.

question_or_heading: A company has net income of ₹20,00,000 and total assets of ₹2,00,00,000. What is its ROA?
hint: ROA = Net Income ÷ Total Assets.
explanation: ₹20,00,000 ÷ ₹2,00,00,000 = 0.10, or 10% — the company generates 10 paise of profit for every rupee of assets it holds.

question_or_heading: A capital-light software company and a capital-heavy airline post identical net income. Which would you generally expect to have the HIGHER ROA?
option_a: The airline, since planes are valuable assets
option_b: The software company, since it needs far fewer total assets to generate the same profit
option_c: They'll always be identical
option_d: ROA doesn't apply to service businesses
hint: Which company needs a much smaller denominator (total assets) to generate the same profit?
explanation: With far fewer assets required to generate the same profit, the software company would post a meaningfully higher ROA — even with identical net income to the asset-heavy airline.

question_or_heading: ROA accounts for how a company's assets happen to be financed — with debt or with equity.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does the ROA formula involve liabilities or equity at all?
explanation: ROA only involves net income and total assets — it deliberately ignores HOW those assets were financed, which is exactly why ROE (the next lesson) exists as a complementary measure.

question_or_heading: Two companies have identical total assets, but Company X's net income is double Company Y's. What does this tell you about their relative ROA?
option_a: Company X's ROA will be double Company Y's
option_b: Company Y's ROA will be double Company X's
option_c: Their ROA will be identical
option_d: ROA has no relationship to net income
hint: With the same denominator, what happens to the ratio when the numerator doubles?
explanation: With identical total assets (the denominator) but double the net income (the numerator), Company X's ROA comes out exactly double Company Y's.

question_or_heading: Why might comparing ROA across two companies in very different industries be misleading, similar to the earlier gross margin caution?
option_a: ROA is identical across all industries, so comparisons are always valid
option_b: Different industries have structurally different asset intensity — a capital-heavy manufacturer will typically show lower ROA than a capital-light service business, regardless of actual management quality
option_c: ROA only applies to manufacturing companies
option_d: There's no meaningful difference between industries for ROA purposes
hint: Recall the earlier caution about comparing gross margins across very different industries — does the same logic apply here?
explanation: Just as with gross margin, structural differences in how asset-intensive an industry naturally is can make cross-industry ROA comparisons misleading — ROA is most meaningful when comparing companies within the same or similar industries.

question_or_heading: How much profit per rupee of owners' investment?
option_a: Return on Equity = Net Income ÷ Total Equity. It measures the return generated specifically for shareholders, on the capital they've contributed and the profits the company has retained.

question_or_heading: Debt can inflate ROE
option_a: A company using more debt (and less equity) to finance its assets can show a higher ROE than an equally profitable company using less debt — because the same net income is divided by a smaller equity base.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Return on Equity = Net Income ÷ Total Equity — the return generated specifically for shareholders on their invested and retained capital.

question_or_heading: A company has net income of ₹15,00,000 and total equity of ₹75,00,000. What is its ROE?
hint: ROE = Net Income ÷ Total Equity.
explanation: ₹15,00,000 ÷ ₹75,00,000 = 0.20, or 20% — shareholders are earning a 20% return on their stake in the company that year.

question_or_heading: Two companies have identical net income and identical total assets, but Company A uses much more debt (and less equity) to finance those assets than Company B. Which would you expect to have the HIGHER ROE?
option_a: Company B, with more equity
option_b: Company A, with less equity funding the same asset base, and therefore a smaller ROE denominator
option_c: They'll always be identical
option_d: ROE is unaffected by financing choices
hint: With a smaller equity base (denominator) but the same net income (numerator), what happens to the ratio?
explanation: With a smaller equity base absorbing the same net income, Company A's ROE would come out higher — a direct illustration of how leverage (debt) can amplify ROE, for better or worse.

question_or_heading: A very high ROE is always unambiguously a sign of a great, low-risk business.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Could a high ROE be driven by heavy debt rather than genuinely great underlying profitability?
explanation: As the leverage example shows, a high ROE can be partly or largely driven by heavy debt financing rather than pure operating excellence — meaning it should be interpreted alongside debt levels, not read as unambiguously positive on its own.

question_or_heading: Why do analysts often look at ROA and ROE TOGETHER, rather than relying on just one of them?
option_a: Because ROA and ROE always give identical results, so checking both is redundant
option_b: Because comparing the two can reveal how much of a company's shareholder return is coming from genuine asset efficiency versus financial leverage (debt)
option_c: ROA and ROE measure completely unrelated things with no useful comparison
option_d: Only ROE is ever relevant; ROA is a purely academic concept
hint: What does the GAP between ROA and ROE specifically reveal about a company's financing choices?
explanation: A large gap between ROA (unaffected by financing) and ROE (which leverage can inflate) is itself informative — it points toward how much of the shareholder return is coming from real asset efficiency versus simply the amplifying effect of debt.

question_or_heading: A company boosts its ROE significantly by taking on much more debt, with net income and total assets staying roughly the same. What's a reasonable concern to weigh against the improved ROE?
option_a: There's no concern — ROE improving is always unambiguously good news
option_b: The company now carries more financial risk (from the earlier capital structure unit), which isn't visible just by looking at the improved ROE number alone
option_c: This is mathematically impossible without a change in net income
option_d: Debt has no bearing on financial risk
hint: Recall the capital structure and leverage lessons from Book V — what risk does more debt introduce, that a rising ROE number alone doesn't show?
explanation: As covered in the earlier capital structure lessons, more debt raises financial risk (bigger fixed obligations, more exposure if performance dips) — risk that a rising ROE figure alone doesn't reveal, which is exactly why ROE should never be read in isolation.

question_or_heading: How much revenue per rupee of assets?
option_a: Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets. It measures how efficiently a company uses its total asset base to generate sales — a pure efficiency measure, not a profitability one.

question_or_heading: Different from ROA, on purpose
option_a: ROA asks 'how much PROFIT per rupee of assets.' Asset turnover asks 'how much REVENUE per rupee of assets' — related, but measuring efficiency at a different stage.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets — how efficiently a company generates sales from the assets it owns, independent of profit margin.

question_or_heading: A company has revenue of ₹3,00,00,000 and total assets of ₹1,50,00,000. What is its asset turnover?
option_c: 2x
option_d: 3x
hint: Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets.
explanation: ₹3,00,00,000 ÷ ₹1,50,00,000 = 2x — the company generates ₹2 of revenue for every ₹1 of assets it holds.

question_or_heading: A grocery retailer (low margins, high sales volume) and a luxury jeweler (high margins, low sales volume) would typically differ most in which ratio?
option_a: Net margin only, with asset turnover being identical
option_b: Asset turnover — the grocery retailer likely turns over its assets much faster, generating more sales per rupee of assets, even with thinner margins
option_c: Neither ratio would differ between these two business models
option_d: Total assets, which is unrelated to either ratio
hint: Which business model relies on selling a lot, fast, versus selling less, for more, per item?
explanation: High-volume, low-margin retail typically posts much higher asset turnover than a slower-moving, high-margin business like luxury jewelry — a classic contrast in how different business models hit similar profitability through very different paths.

question_or_heading: Asset turnover measures profitability directly, in the same way ROA does.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does the asset turnover formula involve net income at all?
explanation: Asset turnover uses revenue, not net income — it's a pure efficiency measure of sales generation, distinct from ROA's profitability focus, even though both use total assets as the denominator.

question_or_heading: A company's asset turnover declines significantly year over year, while revenue stays flat. What does this most likely indicate?
option_a: Nothing — asset turnover is unrelated to revenue
option_b: The company's total assets grew significantly without a matching increase in revenue, making it less efficient at generating sales from its asset base
option_c: Revenue must have declined as well
option_d: This combination is mathematically impossible
hint: If revenue (the numerator) stayed flat, what must have happened to the denominator (total assets) for the ratio to fall?
explanation: With flat revenue but a shrinking turnover ratio, total assets must have grown without generating proportionally more sales — the company is becoming less efficient at converting its (growing) asset base into revenue.

question_or_heading: Why might a company with relatively low profit MARGINS still deliver strong overall returns to shareholders?
option_a: Low margins always guarantee poor overall returns, with no exceptions
option_b: High asset turnover (or high leverage) can compensate for thin margins — a business can be very profitable overall by selling a lot, efficiently, even at a lower margin per sale
option_c: Margins are the only factor that ever matters for overall returns
option_d: This combination is impossible in any real business
hint: Recall the grocery-retailer-versus-jeweler contrast — can strong efficiency compensate for a thinner margin?
explanation: As the grocery-versus-jewelry contrast illustrated, strong efficiency (high asset turnover) can offset a thinner margin — foreshadowing the next lesson's DuPont framework, which formally ties margin, turnover, and leverage together into overall return.

question_or_heading: How fast does inventory move?
option_a: Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory. It measures how many times a company sells through and replaces its inventory over a period — higher generally means faster-moving, fresher stock.

question_or_heading: Too high or too low both raise questions
option_a: Very low turnover can mean slow-moving, obsolete, or overstocked inventory. Very high turnover, in some cases, can mean the company is understocked and risking missed sales.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory — how many times a company cycles through its inventory in a period.

question_or_heading: A company has COGS of ₹80,00,000 and average inventory of ₹20,00,000. What is its inventory turnover?
option_b: 2x
option_c: 4x
option_d: 8x
hint: Inventory Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Inventory.
explanation: ₹80,00,000 ÷ ₹20,00,000 = 4x — the company cycles through (sells and replaces) its entire inventory roughly 4 times over the period.

question_or_heading: A retailer's inventory turnover falls sharply from 6x last year to 2x this year, with no major business changes announced. What might this suggest?
option_a: Nothing worth investigating
option_b: Inventory may be moving much more slowly, possibly signaling weakening demand or overstocking — worth digging into further
option_c: This always means the retailer is thriving
option_d: Turnover ratios never change meaningfully year to year
hint: Is slower inventory turnover generally a sign of healthier or weaker sales momentum, all else equal?
explanation: A sharp turnover slowdown often points to inventory piling up faster than it's selling — echoing the balance sheet red flags lesson's caution about rising inventory without matching sales growth.

question_or_heading: A higher inventory turnover ratio generally indicates inventory is moving through the business faster.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does more 'turns' per period mean faster or slower cycling through inventory?
explanation: More turns in the same period directly means inventory is being sold and replenished faster — the core meaning of a higher turnover ratio.

question_or_heading: Why might comparing inventory turnover between a fresh-produce grocer and a furniture retailer be misleading without industry context?
option_a: It wouldn't be misleading at all — turnover always means the same thing everywhere
option_b: Perishable, fast-moving goods naturally turn over far more often than large, considered purchases like furniture, making cross-industry comparison unfair without adjusting for that difference
option_c: Furniture retailers never hold any inventory
option_d: Grocers never track inventory turnover
hint: Which of these two business types would naturally sell through stock much faster, purely due to the nature of the product, regardless of management quality?
explanation: Perishable groceries naturally turn over far more frequently than furniture, purely due to product nature — comparing the two directly, without industry context, would unfairly make one look far more 'efficient' than the other.

question_or_heading: A company's inventory turnover is extremely high, well above its industry peers, but customers frequently complain about popular items being out of stock. What might this specific combination suggest?
option_a: Nothing concerning — extremely high turnover is always purely positive
option_b: The company might be understocking to keep turnover numbers looking good, at the cost of actually meeting customer demand and potentially losing sales
option_c: Stockouts and turnover ratios are completely unrelated
option_d: This combination proves the company is committing fraud
hint: Recall the intro card's caution about turnover being 'too high' — what real-world cost might extremely lean inventory carry?
explanation: As flagged in the intro, unusually high turnover paired with stockout complaints suggests the company may be running inventory too lean — optimizing the ratio at the real cost of lost sales and unhappy customers.

question_or_heading: How fast are customers paying?
option_a: Receivables Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Accounts Receivable. It measures how many times a company collects its full receivables balance over a period — higher generally means faster collections.

question_or_heading: Turning it into days is often more intuitive
option_a: Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) = 365 ÷ Receivables Turnover. It converts the ratio into 'roughly how many days does it take to collect from a typical sale,' which is easier to picture.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Receivables Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Receivables — how many times a company collects its receivables balance in a period; converting to days (DSO) makes it easier to interpret.

question_or_heading: A company has revenue of ₹1,00,00,000 and average accounts receivable of ₹25,00,000. What is its receivables turnover?
option_b: 2x
option_c: 4x
hint: Receivables Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Receivables.
explanation: ₹1,00,00,000 ÷ ₹25,00,000 = 4x — the company effectively collects its outstanding receivables balance about 4 times over the year.

question_or_heading: A company's receivables turnover is 6x per year. Approximately how many days (DSO) does it take, on average, to collect payment after a sale?
option_a: 6 days
option_b: 30 days
option_c: 61 days
option_d: 180 days
hint: DSO = 365 ÷ Receivables Turnover.
explanation: 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 61 days — on average, it takes the company a bit over two months to actually collect cash after making a credit sale.

question_or_heading: A rising DSO (Days Sales Outstanding) generally indicates customers are paying faster than before.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does more DAYS to collect mean faster or slower collections?
explanation: A rising DSO means MORE days are needed to collect — the opposite of faster; rising DSO signals slower, not faster, collections.

question_or_heading: A company's revenue grows 15% this year, but its DSO also jumps from 40 days to 70 days. What connects directly back to an earlier lesson in this course?
option_a: Nothing — this is unrelated to anything covered previously
option_b: This mirrors the balance sheet red flag and cash flow lessons about receivables growing faster than revenue — a sign sales may be outpacing the company's ability to actually collect cash
option_c: This combination is mathematically impossible
option_d: Revenue growth always improves DSO automatically
hint: Recall the balance sheet red flags and working capital changes lessons — what did rapidly growing receivables, relative to revenue, tend to suggest there?
explanation: A sharply worsening DSO alongside revenue growth is exactly the receivables-outpacing-revenue pattern flagged as a red flag earlier in this course — this ratio just gives it a precise, trackable number.

question_or_heading: Why might a company deliberately loosen its credit terms (giving customers more time to pay) even knowing it will worsen DSO?
option_a: There's never a legitimate reason to do this
option_b: It might be a deliberate strategy to boost sales by making purchases easier for customers, accepting a trade-off of slower cash collection for higher revenue
option_c: DSO is unrelated to credit terms
option_d: Loosening credit terms always improves DSO
hint: Could there be a legitimate business reason — beyond a purely negative story — for choosing to accept slower collections?
explanation: Offering more generous payment terms can be a deliberate lever to win more sales — a real trade-off between growth and collection speed, not automatically a red flag, though it's exactly the kind of context an analyst needs to judge.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: The mirror image, for suppliers
option_a: Payables Turnover = COGS ÷ Average Accounts Payable, measuring how quickly a company pays its own suppliers — converted to days (Days Payable Outstanding, DPO), it shows roughly how long the company takes to pay.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: Putting the whole cycle together
option_a: Cash Conversion Cycle = Days Inventory Outstanding + Days Sales Outstanding − Days Payable Outstanding. It measures how many days cash is tied up, from paying for inventory to collecting from customers.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: The cash conversion cycle combines inventory days, collection days, and payment days into one number: how long cash is tied up in the operating cycle.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: A company's inventory sits for 40 days on average (DIO), customers take 30 days to pay (DSO), and the company takes 25 days to pay its own suppliers (DPO). What is its cash conversion cycle?
option_a: 95 days
option_b: 70 days
option_c: 45 days
option_d: 5 days
hint: Cash Conversion Cycle = DIO + DSO − DPO.
explanation: 40 + 30 − 25 = 45 days — roughly how long, on average, cash is tied up from paying for inventory until it's finally collected back from a customer.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: A company manages to extend how long it takes to pay its own suppliers (higher DPO), with DIO and DSO unchanged. What happens to its cash conversion cycle?
option_a: It increases
option_b: It decreases, since a higher DPO is subtracted in the formula
option_c: It's unaffected
option_d: The formula becomes invalid
hint: In the formula DIO + DSO − DPO, what happens to the total when the subtracted term gets bigger?
explanation: Since DPO is subtracted, a longer time to pay suppliers actually shortens the cash conversion cycle — the company effectively uses supplier credit to fund more of its own operating cycle.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: A negative cash conversion cycle is impossible in any real business.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the earlier lesson on negative working capital retailers — could DPO ever exceed DIO plus DSO?
explanation: Some businesses (like certain fast-turning retailers, echoing the earlier negative-working-capital example) genuinely achieve a negative cash conversion cycle — collecting from customers and even reinvesting before their own supplier payments are due.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: Why is a SHORTER cash conversion cycle generally considered favorable for a business?
option_a: Shorter is always worse, since it means less time to plan
option_b: It means less cash is tied up in the operating cycle for a shorter period, freeing that cash up for other uses sooner
option_c: The cash conversion cycle has no real business implications
option_d: Shorter cycles always indicate declining sales
hint: What does 'shorter' mean in terms of how long a company's own cash is stuck funding its inventory-to-collection cycle?
explanation: A shorter cash conversion cycle means the company's cash is tied up for less time between paying for inventory and collecting from customers — freeing that cash up sooner for other productive uses, which is generally a sign of operational efficiency.

lesson_title: Payables Turnover & the Cash Conversion Cycle
question_or_heading: Two companies have identical DIO and DSO, but Company A has a much higher DPO than Company B. What does this suggest about their relative cash conversion cycles and working capital efficiency?
option_a: They'll be identical, since DPO doesn't matter
option_b: Company A will have a shorter cash conversion cycle, effectively using supplier financing more aggressively than Company B to reduce how much of its own cash is tied up
option_c: Company B will always have the shorter cycle
option_d: DPO has no bearing on the cash conversion cycle
hint: With identical DIO and DSO, which company is subtracting a bigger number (DPO) from the total?
explanation: With the same inventory and collection timelines, Company A's higher DPO — subtracted in the formula — gives it the shorter, more cash-efficient cycle, effectively leaning more on supplier financing to fund its operations.

question_or_heading: Breaking ROE into three drivers
option_a: DuPont analysis splits ROE into three components multiplied together: Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage (Total Assets ÷ Equity) — revealing WHERE a company's return is actually coming from.

question_or_heading: Same ROE, very different stories
option_a: Two companies can post the exact same ROE for completely different reasons — one through fat margins, another through fast turnover, a third mostly through heavy leverage — and DuPont is what tells them apart.

question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: DuPont analysis breaks ROE into Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage — showing whether a company's returns come from profitability, efficiency, or debt.

question_or_heading: A company has a net margin of 10%, asset turnover of 1.5x, and financial leverage (assets/equity) of 2x. Using DuPont analysis, what is its approximate ROE?
hint: ROE = Net Margin × Asset Turnover × Financial Leverage.
explanation: 0.10 × 1.5 × 2 = 0.30, or 30% — DuPont breaks that 30% ROE down into exactly which three factors combined to produce it.

question_or_heading: Two companies both post a 25% ROE. Company A gets there mainly through a high net margin; Company B gets there mainly through very high financial leverage. Which would you generally view as carrying more financial risk, all else equal?
option_a: Company A, from the strong margin
option_b: Company B, since heavy reliance on leverage to drive ROE means more debt and more financial risk
option_c: Neither carries any more risk than the other
option_d: ROE alone always tells you everything about risk
hint: Recall the leverage-and-ROE lesson — what risk does relying heavily on debt (leverage) to boost ROE carry, that a margin-driven ROE doesn't?
explanation: Even with identical headline ROE, Company B's return is propped up more by debt-fueled leverage — carrying the added financial risk flagged in the earlier ROE lesson, risk that isn't visible from the ROE number alone but IS visible once you break it down with DuPont.

question_or_heading: DuPont analysis reveals that two companies with the identical headline ROE could be getting there through very different underlying combinations of margin, turnover, and leverage.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Is DuPont's whole purpose to show you the ROE number itself, or to explain what's driving it?
explanation: That's exactly DuPont's purpose: the same ROE number can hide very different underlying stories, and breaking it into its three components is what reveals which story is actually true.

question_or_heading: Why is DuPont analysis considered a more insightful tool than looking at ROE alone?
option_a: It isn't more insightful — ROE alone is always sufficient
option_b: It decomposes a single summary number into three distinct, more diagnosable drivers — profitability, efficiency, and leverage — pointing an analyst toward exactly where to dig deeper
option_c: DuPont analysis and ROE are the exact same calculation with no real difference
option_d: DuPont analysis only works for very large companies
hint: What does breaking one number into three separate drivers let an analyst do that the single combined number doesn't?
explanation: By splitting one summary number into three distinct, individually diagnosable drivers, DuPont points an analyst toward exactly which lever — margin, turnover, or leverage — is really behind a company's return, rather than leaving that story hidden inside a single combined figure.

question_or_heading: A company's ROE has improved significantly, but a DuPont breakdown shows its net margin and asset turnover are both essentially unchanged. What must be driving the improvement?
option_a: Financial leverage must have increased — that's the only remaining factor in the formula
option_b: This improvement must be a calculation error, since nothing else could explain it
option_c: Revenue must have declined
option_d: This scenario is mathematically impossible
hint: With margin and turnover unchanged, which of the three multiplied factors is left to explain a rising overall ROE?
explanation: Since ROE = Margin × Turnover × Leverage, and two of those three factors are unchanged, the improvement can only be coming from the third: rising financial leverage — exactly the kind of insight DuPont is built to surface.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: Two different questions
option_a: Profitability asks 'how much profit per rupee of sales (or assets, or equity)?' Efficiency asks 'how well is the company using its resources to generate activity in the first place?' — related, but genuinely different questions.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: A business can be efficient but not very profitable, or vice versa
option_a: A high-turnover, thin-margin retailer can be highly efficient at moving inventory while still being only modestly profitable. A slow-moving luxury brand can be highly profitable per sale while turning over its assets much more slowly.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Profitability measures how much profit is earned; efficiency measures how well resources are used to generate activity — a business can score high on one and only moderate on the other.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: A discount retailer has thin net margins (3%) but very high asset turnover (5x), while a luxury brand has fat net margins (25%) but low asset turnover (0.8x). Which statement is most accurate?
option_a: The retailer is unprofitable and the luxury brand is inefficient
option_b: Both can be viable, successful businesses — the retailer emphasizes efficiency (fast turnover) while the luxury brand emphasizes profitability (fat margins) as their respective paths to strong overall returns
option_c: One of these two business models must be fundamentally flawed
option_d: Efficiency and profitability always move in the same direction together
hint: Recall the DuPont framework — can very different combinations of margin and turnover both add up to a strong overall return?
explanation: This is exactly the DuPont insight in action: very different combinations of margin (profitability) and turnover (efficiency) can each be a legitimate, successful path to strong overall returns — neither approach is inherently superior.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: Which of these ratios primarily measures PROFITABILITY, rather than efficiency?
option_a: Asset turnover
option_b: Inventory turnover
option_c: Net margin
option_d: Receivables turnover
hint: Which of these directly involves a profit figure, versus a pure activity/volume measure?
explanation: Net margin, dividing profit by revenue, is squarely a profitability measure — while the other three (turnover ratios) measure activity and efficiency, without a profit figure involved at all.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: A company can have excellent efficiency ratios (fast turnover) while still posting weak overall profitability, if its margins are thin enough.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Recall the discount retailer example — can high turnover coexist with only modest overall profit margins?
explanation: As the discount retailer example showed, strong efficiency (fast turnover) doesn't automatically guarantee strong profitability — thin margins can still leave overall profitability modest, even with excellent efficiency.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: An analyst is evaluating a company and finds strong efficiency ratios but weak profitability ratios. What's a sensible next step?
option_a: Conclude the company is a bad investment with no further analysis needed
option_b: Investigate WHY margins are thin despite good efficiency — perhaps intense competition, high input costs, or a deliberate low-price strategy — since efficiency alone doesn't guarantee attractive returns
option_c: Ignore the efficiency ratios entirely, since they don't matter
option_d: Assume the ratios must be miscalculated
hint: Should a mixed result — good on one dimension, weak on the other — end the analysis, or prompt more digging into the 'why'?
explanation: A mixed result like this is exactly a prompt for deeper investigation into what's suppressing margins despite good operational efficiency — competition, costs, or strategy — rather than an automatic verdict either way.

lesson_title: Efficiency vs. Profitability: Not the Same Thing
question_or_heading: Why does distinguishing between profitability and efficiency matter when diagnosing what's driving — or holding back — a company's overall returns?
option_a: It doesn't matter; they're interchangeable concepts that always tell the same story
option_b: Because the right fix for a profitability problem (e.g., raise prices, cut costs) is very different from the right fix for an efficiency problem (e.g., reduce excess inventory, collect faster) — correctly diagnosing which one is weak matters for what comes next
option_c: Only profitability is ever relevant to diagnosing a company's performance
option_d: Efficiency and profitability ratios always move in perfect lockstep
hint: If a company's returns are weak, does it matter whether the root cause is a margin problem or a turnover problem, in terms of what should actually be done about it?
explanation: Correctly diagnosing WHICH dimension — profitability or efficiency — is actually underperforming matters enormously, since the appropriate response (pricing and cost decisions versus asset and working capital management) is completely different depending on which one is really the problem.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Bringing the whole toolkit together
option_a: This capstone pulls together margins, ROA, ROE, asset turnover, inventory turnover, receivables turnover, the cash conversion cycle, and DuPont — the full profitability-and-efficiency toolkit from this unit.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Numbers alone don't diagnose — context does
option_a: The real skill isn't calculating each ratio correctly (important as that is) — it's comparing two companies' ratios side by side and building a coherent story about what's actually driving the differences.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Key phrase
option_a: Comparing companies well means calculating the right ratios, then asking what story the pattern across ALL of them — margins, turnover, ROE, DuPont — tells together.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Company A has a 20% net margin and 0.5x asset turnover. Company B has a 4% net margin and 5x asset turnover. Both post similar overall ROA. What does this tell you?
option_a: One of these companies must have made a calculation error
option_b: They're reaching similar overall efficiency-adjusted profitability through very different combinations of margin and turnover — echoing the DuPont-style insight from earlier in this unit
option_c: Company A is definitely the better business overall
option_d: Asset turnover is irrelevant if margins are known
hint: Recall the DuPont and profitability-vs-efficiency lessons — can very different margin/turnover combinations land on a similar overall result?
explanation: Just as DuPont revealed for ROE, Company A and Company B are reaching similar overall ROA through very different paths — fat margins with slow turnover, versus thin margins with fast turnover — neither combination inherently superior.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Comparing two retailers, you find Retailer X has a much shorter cash conversion cycle than Retailer Y, despite similar margins. What advantage does this most directly suggest for Retailer X?
option_a: No real advantage — cash conversion cycle is a meaningless metric
option_b: Retailer X likely has less cash tied up in its operating cycle at any given time, freeing up cash for other uses sooner than Retailer Y
option_c: Retailer X must have lower total revenue
option_d: This means Retailer X is definitely less profitable
hint: Recall the cash conversion cycle lesson — what does a shorter cycle mean for how much of a company's cash is tied up, and for how long?
explanation: A shorter cash conversion cycle, even with similar margins, means Retailer X ties up less cash for less time in its day-to-day operating cycle — a genuine efficiency edge over Retailer Y, distinct from profitability.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: A thorough comparison of two companies' profitability and efficiency should look at multiple ratios together, rather than relying on any single ratio alone.
option_a: True
option_b: False
hint: Does any single ratio in this unit tell the complete story on its own?
explanation: As this whole unit has built toward, no single ratio — margin, ROA, ROE, or any turnover measure — tells the complete story alone; a thorough comparison weighs several together.

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: Pulling together this entire unit — margins, ROA, ROE, turnover ratios, cash conversion cycle, and DuPont — what's the core analytical skill it has built?
option_a: The ability to memorize formulas without understanding what they reveal
option_b: The ability to select the right ratios for a specific question, calculate them correctly, and weave the results together into a coherent story about how a company generates its returns
option_c: The ability to guarantee which of two companies will have a higher future stock price
option_d: No transferable skill — each ratio must be considered in total isolation from the others
hint: What has this unit built beyond just the ability to calculate each individual formula correctly?

lesson_title: Capstone: Comparing Two Companies' Profitability & Efficiency
question_or_heading: You're told Company A has a higher ROE than Company B, but nothing else. Based on this whole unit, what's the correct next step before declaring Company A the 'better' business?
option_a: Immediately declare Company A superior, since ROE is the only ratio that ever matters
option_b: Run a DuPont breakdown and check the other ratios (margins, turnover, cash conversion cycle) to understand WHERE that higher ROE is coming from before drawing any conclusion
option_c: Assume the ROE figures must be wrong, since nothing else is known yet
option_d: Ignore ROE entirely from this point forward
hint: Recall the DuPont lesson's whole point — does a single ROE number, by itself, tell you enough to declare a winner?
explanation: Exactly as DuPont analysis exists to reveal, a higher ROE alone doesn't tell you whether it's coming from genuinely stronger margins and efficiency, or simply more financial leverage and risk — this whole unit's toolkit exists precisely to answer that question properly before drawing a conclusion.
